title: The Forgotten Hindu Temple on Iran’s Coast — and the Indian Merchants Who Built It
excerpt: Amitabh Bachchan’s viral post about a 134-year-old Vishnu temple in Bandar Abbas has surfaced a remarkable chapter of India’s maritime trading diaspora
body:
When Amitabh Bachchan posted a short video of a little-known Hindu temple in southern Iran last week, he inadvertently surfaced one of the most compelling — and least discussed — chapters of India’s commercial diaspora. The Vishnu Temple in Bandar Abbas, perched on the edge of the Persian Gulf in Iran’s Hormozgan Province, has stood since 1892. It was built not by kings or conquerors, but by merchants from Shikarpur, in what is now Pakistan’s Sindh province, who traded in spices, textiles, and dreams along one of the world’s oldest maritime corridors.

## A Temple Born of Trade

The temple was constructed during the Qajar era under the governorship of Mohammad Hassan Khan Sa’d-ol-Malek, the ruler of Bandar Abbas. Hindu merchants from the Indian subcontinent — part of a broader Sindhi trading network that stretched from Astrakhan to Hong Kong — pooled donations to build a place of worship in their adopted port city. The result was a circular structure topped with a distinctive conical dome, ringed by 72 turrets and decorated with muqarnas — the honeycomb-like vaulting technique quintessentially Persian in origin. Inside, paintings of Krishna and other Hindu deities once shared wall space with motifs that blended Indian iconography and Islamic geometric patterns.

The architectural hybrid was deliberate. These were traders who understood that survival in a foreign land meant weaving yourself into its fabric without losing your own thread. The temple stood as a quiet assertion: you could be devout and diplomatic at the same time.

## The Merchants Who Built It

The Shikarpuri merchants were among the most successful trading communities of the 19th century. Operating under the loose umbrella of the British East India Company’s influence in the Persian Gulf, they served as financiers, money-changers, and commodity traders across a vast network linking Bombay, Karachi, Muscat, and the Iranian coast. At their peak, Shikarpuri bankers held the equivalent of modern correspondent-banking relationships across the Gulf. The temple was as much a community centre and dispute-resolution forum as a house of worship — a pattern familiar to anyone who has visited a gurdwara in Southall or a Hindu temple in Jackson Heights.

By the mid-20th century, as trade routes shifted and Partition redrew borders, the Indian merchant community in Bandar Abbas dwindled. Many of the temple’s idols were removed as families departed. The building fell into disuse, its walls fading, its courtyard quieting.

## Preservation — and the Questions It Raises

Today, the Vishnu Temple is protected as a historical monument by Iran’s Cultural Heritage Organisation and operates partly as the Anthropology Museum of the Persian Gulf. Iranian authorities have undertaken some restoration, and a team from India has reportedly been involved in preservation planning. On TripAdvisor, visitors describe “faded grandeur” and “neglected beauty” — phrases that could apply to half the heritage sites across the subcontinent itself.

Bachchan’s post, accompanied by a Persian song, drew thousands of comments from Indians surprised that a Hindu temple exists in the Islamic Republic at all. The astonishment itself is revealing. India and Iran shared a land border until 1947. Zoroastrian refugees from Persia shaped Bombay’s skyline. The two civilisations traded gods and grammar for millennia — the very word “Hindu” derives from the Persian name for the Indus river. Yet popular imagination, shaped by decades of geopolitical estrangement, has all but erased this intimacy.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For NRIs, the Bandar Abbas temple is a mirror held up to their own experience. The Shikarpuri merchants who built it were, in every meaningful sense, the original Non-Resident Indians — adapting to foreign legal systems, negotiating with local power, building community institutions far from home, and wondering how many generations the hyphen in “Indo-Iranian” could hold.

As India and Iran tentatively rebuild diplomatic and economic ties — with the Chabahar port agreement and energy cooperation as centrepieces — the Vishnu Temple stands as physical proof that this is a reconnection, not a new connection. The merchants of Bandar Abbas knew something that foreign-policy analysts are only now rediscovering: that the Persian Gulf was once as much an Indian ocean as an Arabian one.
